title: Enterprises pay $100,000 a day for AI they never ordered
raw_text: Enterprises deploying large language models (LLMs) in production may be unknowingly footing the bill for someone else’s AI business. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) is warning of financially motivated LLMjacking campaigns in which cybercriminals hijack enterprise cloud and model access before reselling it through underground subscription services. The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post . In some incidents, cumulative charges reached $1 million before organizations revoked the compromised access. “LLM Mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a service for paying customers, while the victim’s systems continue accepting requests through credentials they recognize,” said Piyush Sharma , co-founder and CEO at Tuskira. “That puts a lot of weight on the authority attached to each credential. A key issued for one application shouldn’t become a reusable pass to other models and workloads.” GTIG’s analysis is based on multiple incidents in 2026, spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers across North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Stolen model access becomes an underground business GTIG said the monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, criminal routing gateways that aggregate compromised API credentials and resell model access to underground subscribers. These services proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption and hide the original source of access. Multiple operations were identified using open-source gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials. One threat actor, UNC6993, used tools including new-api and gcli2api to aggregate stolen keys and distribute requests across accounts. Another operation used stolen third-party API keys to power Jet Night, a legitimate token-routing service that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in under eight hours, GTIG said. The activity passed nearly $1 million in token costs to the victim organization. Jet Night advertises unlimited access to frontier models for approximately $60 a month, substantially lower than the typical cost of comparable legitimate access. Jet Night also experienced occasional outages that GTIG suspects were caused by victims discovering compromises and revoking keys. “Selling stolen model access gives criminals a reason to keep that access working for as long as possible, which makes the quiet activity before the spending spike especially important,” said Nick Tausek , lead security automation architect at Swimlane. “By the time someone asks why the cloud bill has exploded, the attacker may already have paying customers.” The attack begins long before the bill arrives Initial access involves exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, service account keys, GitHub personal access tokens, and active session tokens, GTIG pointed out. Attackers also harvest LLM API keys from public repositories and scan for exposed model endpoints. Attackers were seen validating stolen keys with minimal single-token requests, sometimes using max-tokens=1. Such micro-transactions can confirm whether credentials work while remaining below conventional consumption-based detection thresholds. “Testing a stolen key with a single-token request barely registers as consumption,” Tausek said. “But pair that request with a newly created credential or an unexpected permission change, and there’s something worth investigating.” Analysts shouldn’t have to pull those connections together manually while the attacker gets a head start, he added. After establishing access, attackers enumerate cloud services, repositories, and data stores for additional credentials. They may escalate privileges, create unauthorized service accounts, inject SSH keys, or establish persistence through compromised workloads. GTIG observed a follow-on threat actor exploiting a user ID rebinding vulnerability in the LiteLLM gateway to elevate ordinary virtual keys into administrative credentials. Sharma said organizations must restrict credentials to their intended models, workloads, and endpoints. “The gateway compromise described in these incidents deserves particular attention,” he said, warning that control of the routing layer could open access beyond the original compromised credential. GTIG recommends tighter credential management, least-privilege permissions, granular API key scopes, monitoring for suspicious low-volume requests, and spending limits on model consumption. It also urges organizations to monitor unauthorized AI service enablement and gateway vulnerabilities.

The activity can generate fake cloud charges exceeding $100,000 in a single day, GTIG said in a blog post . title: Armed with AI, hackers target endpoint security blind spots, raising stakes for CISOs
raw_text: A China-linked hacking group’s use of AI agents to identify security weaknesses during a global espionage campaign is raising concerns about whether enterprises can detect gaps in their defenses before automated attacks exploit them. CrowdStrike reported that the group, tracked as VAPOR PANDA, used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over an 11-day period beginning October 17. The organizations included government agencies and businesses across at least 14 countries, with researchers confirming post-exploitation activity at nine. At a global pharmaceutical company, the attackers instructed AI agents to examine running processes and folder listings on Windows machines to determine whether CrowdStrike’s Falcon sensor was installed, according to transcripts recovered by the cybersecurity firm. ARTEX uses multiple AI agents to carry out intrusion tasks under human direction. CrowdStrike found that VAPOR PANDA used the framework to pursue attacks against several organizations simultaneously, with operators intervening at key decision points. The findings follow an October 21 report from Microsoft detailing a separate campaign involving ARTEX. Microsoft said another China-linked group, Storm-0940 , used the framework to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations, gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours in some cases. The campaign included the abuse of compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access customer environments. Changing economics of cyberattacks The use of AI in cyberattacks is changing the economics of state-sponsored espionage by allowing smaller teams to pursue targets without a corresponding increase in personnel, according to Akshat Tyagi , associate practice leader at HFS Research. “The techniques are familiar, but the ability to run them in parallel is not,” Tyagi said. Jonathan Ong , senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia, said AI can substantially reduce the time attackers spend on reconnaissance, even as more sophisticated exploitation continues to require technical expertise. The attacks documented by CrowdStrike exploited weaknesses that security teams have encountered for years. At a Greek government organization, attackers used authentication keys from a 2022 directory export that had likely not been rotated. At a US pharmaceutical company, an AI agent combined an unsigned SAML assertion with an XML external entity (XXE) vulnerability to obtain a cloud role with extensive administrative permissions. Security gaps become a bigger target Growing concerns about the security risks of AI adoption should not distract organizations from established defensive measures, Ong said. Tyagi added that CISOs should ensure that security monitoring extends across their environments rather than assuming existing deployments provide complete coverage. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations should continuously measure endpoint protection coverage, including on internal servers, and generate alerts when machines stop reporting to security monitoring systems. He also recommended enforcing SAML signature validation and restricting cloud access privileges. Security teams should watch for closely sequenced authentication attempts and commands that could indicate automated malicious activity, he said. Tyagi also recommended regularly rotating credentials and monitoring unusual account activity, warning that automated attacks leave defenders less time to investigate suspicious behavior. Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis, said gaps between security systems could give attackers opportunities to move through enterprise environments. He recommended improving asset visibility and detecting suspicious activity across systems rather than relying on individual security controls. Prospect of Cobalt Strike-style adoption The use of ARTEX by different threat groups also points to the wider availability of tools capable of automating cyberattacks. CrowdStrike said VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX with DeepSeek and a second commercial AI model. Although the framework’s developer withdrew the original open-source project in October following reports of its misuse, copies and modified versions remain available. Tyagi expects such tools to become more widely adopted by financially motivated cybercriminals over the next 12 months. There is already evidence of broader adoption. In research published in October, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said they had observed financially motivated attackers using ARTEX during data-theft extortion operations, alongside its use by suspected state-linked groups. “AI pentesting frameworks such as ARTEX have the potential to become the Cobalt Strike of the AI era,” said Ong. Cobalt Strike , a commercial penetration-testing tool, has been widely abused by cybercriminals and state-sponsored groups. As attackers automate more of their operations, security teams may need to rely more heavily on automated detection. Tyagi said this would allow analysts to spend less time manually reviewing alerts and concentrate on decisions requiring human judgment. Prabhu said CISOs should prioritize faster, rehearsed incident response rather than simply investing in additional AI tools or expanding security teams. Such preparations could help security teams respond to intrusions in which automated agents explore multiple attack paths before defenders have completed their initial investigation. Although ARTEX can automate much of an intrusion, the observed campaigns still involved human operators directing key decisions. “We are not at fully autonomous attacks yet,” Tyagi said. The continuing role of human operators does not diminish the speed of the attacks. For security teams, the challenge is detecting suspicious activity early enough to prevent automated intrusion attempts from developing into broader compromises.

title: 67% of security leaders say their teams struggle to meet business needs
raw_text: AI, identity-based attacks, and expanding digital operations are putting pressure on already overstretched cybersecurity teams. Security vendor Barracuda’s Cybersecurity Skills Gap report also found that security teams are struggling to keep pace with expanding responsibilities. The vast majority of the 2,000 IT and security decision-makers surveyed report cybersecurity skills gaps. In particular, the most common challenges are linked to AI-related risks (68%) and advanced identity and phishing threats (67%), including business email compromise , OAuth abuse, and multi-factor authentication bypass. Two-thirds (67%) of respondents say security teams are under pressure and struggling to scale to meet evolving business needs. Half say their security professionals are expected to support growing digital operations without additional resources. More than half (56%) report a reduction in security head count linked to AI, split evenly between entry-level and more senior roles. As AI takes on more routine analysis and response activities, human roles are shifting toward (higher value) threat investigation, incident leadership, automation governance, and business risk management. “AI is changing the cybersecurity landscape faster than many security teams can build the necessary skills, visibility, and governance,” said Siroui Mushegian, senior vice president and chief information officer at Barracuda. “Organizations need to reshape their security teams, combining the power of AI and automation with human expertise, judgment, and visibility.” Hiring challenges CSO parent company Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities report found that cloud security (35%), securing agentic AI technology (34%), and securing AI/machine learning-enabled technology (30%) topped the areas CSOs felt their teams needed to become more skilled and knowledgeable about in order to meet overall corporate security objectives. Underlining the difficulty of this ambition, the report found that cloud security architects, AI security specialist, and forensics analysts were the most difficult cybersecurity roles in which to find suitable applicants. Accessing the cost of the skills gap Separately, technology-focused online learning platform Pluralsight’s Tech Skills Report 2026 found that 41% of cybersecurity professionals in the UK estimate skills gaps cost them at least £380,000 each year (US$500,000). This estimated cost includes hiring and outsourcing expenses, lost revenue, abandoned projects, and poorly maintained technology. A quarter of cybersecurity professionals say their organization has experienced security incidents or vulnerabilities over the past 12 months due to skills gaps. Almost half (43%) admitted that skills gaps are a common reason for abandoning cybersecurity projects. The findings highlight the pressure on security teams as AI adoption increases demand for cybersecurity expertise, Pluralsight concludes. AI imperative exacerbating skills problem Europe is short of more than 300,000 cybersecurity professionals, and companies are now struggling to find qualified candidates or applicants, according to research by the AI Workforce Consortium . Cybersecurity job postings requiring AI skills have doubled year over year across G7 countries. Senior cybersecurity roles requiring AI skills are up 65% year-on-year, compared with 5.9% for junior roles. The research by the AI Workforce Consortium — an industry group backed by Cisco, Google, Microsoft, IBM, SAP, and others — also points to a growing need for practical experience and human skills.

title: European supermarkets that failed to act after French freezer attack are now feeling the heat
raw_text: Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday. The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults. In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution. The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report , which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize. No group has as yet claimed to be behind the attacks. A spokesman for Ahold Delhaize told CSO, “On Monday, November 2, we identified an incident affecting refrigeration systems in dozens of Delhaize stores. We immediately took the necessary measures to limit the impact and keep the stores operational.” The situation has since returned to normal, although the company had to discard valuable food, he said. Delay understandable Analysts and consultants said the lack of an immediate response to the initial refrigeration attacks is understandable, given the complex nature of the systems and the multiple vendors who typically manage such systems for major retailers. Gartner Distinguished VP Analyst Katell Thielemann said that although the impacted European retailers own the hardware, they outsource the maintenance, upkeep, and the management. Thus, she said, “there is some confusion about who owns what in this black box of outsourcing.” IDC Senior Research Manager Bobby Kuzma agreed. “There’s a huge gap in visibility between the folks who monitor threat intelligence and vulnerability reports, and the people who manage the OT/industrial side of the universe,” he said. “The cybersecurity teams may not have even been aware that the devices were network connected, especially if they were riding on dedicated internet circuits for manufacturer support.” Thielemann added that the incident was made worse because of the historic lack of priority given to cybersecurity defenses in retail. “It’s proof that cybersecurity is still not top of mind,” she said. “Even when it’s so egregious, senior [retail] leaders are not asking, ‘How do we get ahead of this?’” However, Kuzma argued, this problem comes down to asset inventory visibility. “You can’t protect a system that you don’t know you have. You can’t scan for exposures on a connection that you don’t know exists,” he pointed out. “Sometimes that inventory requires somebody physically going into the telco closet at the locations and asking pointed questions about equipment that’s present. In this day and age, having devices of any type hanging off a public internet connection and accessible is asking for trouble.” IoT handled outside of IT David Neuman , an executive advisor with consulting firm Acceligence, also noted that it was never realistic to assume that issuing a cybersecurity advisory was going to meaningfully address this security hole. “An advisory doesn’t fix a system nobody in the building owns,” Neuman said. “Contractors often install and service store refrigeration controllers under arrangements that rely on a constant data feed, so they can sit outside the security team’s inventory and authority. Taking the controllers offline means finding them, then reworking how the contractor gets in, store by store.” That, he said, “explains the gap, but it doesn’t excuse it: France gave everyone a three-week warning. Abusing a legitimate function like defrost causes physical and financial damage without any malware.” Brian Levine , a partner at consulting firm Control Risks, added that another part of the problem is that IoT devices have always been handled outside of IT. “For years, organizations treated connected operational equipment as a facilities issue. These incidents end that debate,” Levine said. “Security professionals never dismissed this risk; budgets deprioritized it because nothing had failed at scale. Now it has, and boards will ask why vendor contracts, incident response plans, and tabletop exercises never accounted for a physical outcome.” And, said Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520, this issue goes beyond the fact that the attackers could gain access. He said that he is most concerned about the range of things the attackers were able to do with that access. “The attackers could reportedly manipulate refrigeration systems to operate far outside their intended parameters,” Kenney said. “Even if someone gains access to a system, there should be independent safeguards preventing commands that could damage equipment or disrupt operations. The fact that remote access can potentially translate into physical damage suggests some serious gaps in how these systems are designed and secured.” Kenney also noted that some of these devices had long passed their end-of-life, meaning that security patches and other upgrades may have been unavailable. “Organizations can end up relying on equipment that still functions perfectly well operationally, but can no longer be adequately secured,” he pointed out. “That creates difficult decisions about network isolation, compensating controls, and ultimately when equipment needs to be replaced.” Indeed, said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy , some in IT tend to ignore IoT systems, especially when they were deployed by functional units without permission from IT or cybersecurity teams. “Enterprises don’t tend to look at fridges in the same light as servers, smartphones, and other traditionally connected devices,” he noted. “If anything, most IT shops have a limited view of what constitutes a connected device in the first place. That means many organizations are running connected devices, such as appliances, floor cleaners and once-dumb but now increasingly smart machines, with dangerously outdated firmware because they never identified them as connected in the first place.” Unexpected threat to IT As well, said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, there are also corporate legal issues that may undercut cybersecurity’s need for quick action. “CERT-FR’s own alert shows why that takes time. Before cutting a controller off the internet, it tells operators to check the insurance terms in their contract with the refrigeration provider. That one line says a lot,” he said, adding that many of these controllers are installed, monitored, and guaranteed by a contractor who depends on the data feed. The store may have neither the ability nor the authority to shut them down. “Three weeks of warning is a long time for an attacker and a short time for a supermarket chain. Close the door to the internet first and renegotiate the contracts second,” he said. Dickson also argued that these refrigeration attacks pose an unexpected threat to traditional IT systems as well, because servers and other equipment are temperature-sensitive. “An attacker who reaches the building management system does not need to touch a single server. The servers will shut themselves down rather than cook,” Dickson said. “You do not need to hack the data center. You only need to hack the air conditioning.”
summary: Just a couple of weeks after a cyberattack on French supermarket refrigeration systems resulted in spoiled food, and even some fires, retailers in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, Finland, and Estonia were hit with nearly-identical attacks on Monday. The mid-October attack prompted an advisory from the French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) recommending that organizations disconnect any refrigeration control systems with public IP addresses from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults. In an emergency, the advisory suggested, organizations could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution. The Monday attack, like the one in October, “resulted in sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers,” according to a Bloomberg report , which confirmed incidents with impacted retailers, including Carrefour, Spar, and Ahold Delhaize.

title: A compromised DevOps laptop caused the $6.3B Binance breach
raw_text: Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers. “Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization. Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets using company funds, while the remaining 5%, comprising less-liquid tokens, could take longer to source. The exchange said its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised employee device that enabled access to a service container involved in withdrawals. “This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level,” said Tim Rawlins , senior advisor and director of security at NCC Group. “When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities.” The FBI has since attributed the attack to North Korean threat actors, identifying the TraderTraitor hacking group as responsible for the theft. “Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable efforts in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges,” Rawlins said. A compromised laptop reaches the withdrawal pipeline Binance’s preliminary findings suggest that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop before gaining access to a service container and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The exchange has yet to publish technical details of the attack, leaving important questions about the precise intrusion path and how the attackers navigated its internal systems. “A platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security to prevent a single compromise, such as an employee’s laptop being hacked, from being sufficient to authorize a transfer,” said Mario Rivas , blockchain and digital assets security lead at NCC Group. The reported attack is similar to the February 2025 Bybit breach , in which attackers compromised a developer’s machine at Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the interface presented to transaction signers. However, the Binance incident involved a different mechanism. F6’s Threat Intelligence Department (TID) said the Binance attack reportedly targeted an automated withdrawal process rather than directly deceiving authorized signers. Evgeniy Yanov , Head of Audit and Consulting Department at F6, cited Crypto security platform Blockaid, highlighting a batch of 50 EIP-7702 authorizations within a single transaction, alongside delegation to a malicious “sweeper” contract, as an unusual feature of the reported attack. “This specific mechanism has not been seen before in large-scale breaches of this size,” Yanov said. FBI points to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit considered part of the broader Lazarus infrastructure. The agency, working with the US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, said it had observed the attackers converting stolen assets privately into Ethereum. It warned that the funds could subsequently be laundered through decentralized finance platforms and instant-swap services. F6’s TID said the attribution was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain intelligence. “The group’s signature matches previous thefts: small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund the operator’s wallet, extensive preparation well before the actual heist, and pre-signed transactions executed in a single burst,” it added. TID researchers noted similarities with previous North Korean-linked cryptocurrency thefts, including the Bybit and KelpDAO incidents. However, they cautioned that Binance has not independently named the perpetrators and that the full attribution evidence has not been published. Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment. NCC Group’s Rawlins noted that the growing use of AI could help attackers chain vulnerabilities and operational weaknesses together, while organizations increasingly face adversaries willing to invest considerable effort when the potential financial return is substantial. “Good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organizations are still missing,” he said.

It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization. Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP.

title: Cursor removes malicious Claude Code extension after SSH backdoor attempt
raw_text: A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code, credentials and other sensitive information. “Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice . Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29. The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server. “These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic,” Cursor added in the notice. The affected versions were available for Windows and macOS. Anthropic subsequently clarified how the tampered extension had been distributed. In a post on X, Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff, said the incident did not involve a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor had used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish the modified extension, he said. “The versions on our official channels are not affected, and this only impacts Cursor users,” Rieseberg wrote. Anthropic said it was working with Cursor on the incident. Cursor and Anthropic had not responded to requests for comment by publication time. Malware ran without user interaction Security company Phorion, which analysed the compromised extension, found that malicious code had been inserted at the beginning of its JavaScript file. It ran as soon as the extension loaded, before its normal activation code. “The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire,” Phorion said . The malware attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to the user’s authorized_keys file and establish a connection to a remote server. It also created scripts and startup entries intended to keep the connection available after a system restart, the company added. Phorion identified a flaw in the macOS code. The malware tried to check whether Remote Login was disabled using a system command that required administrator privileges. When run without those privileges, the command returned an access error rather than the expected status. The malware consequently skipped the attempt to enable SSH. Phorion also found an error in the Windows code that could prevent its SSH service setup command from running correctly. Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate analysis, detailed the information the malware collected, including machine names, usernames, operating systems, working directories, and Git email addresses. “It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP , keeping up to forty matches,” Microsoft wrote in the analysis. It said the code collected matching variable names, not their values. Removing the extension may not be enough Cursor said enabling the local SSH service would generally fail without administrator privileges on affected Windows and macOS machines. However, the extension could still add the attacker’s SSH key, install persistence mechanisms, and send host information to the attacker. The company warned that uninstalling the extension alone might not remove these components because the malware placed scripts outside the extension’s installation directory. Steve Povolny, vice president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam, said the planted SSH key made cleanup particularly important. “Removing the extension only sends the visitor away while the spare key stays on the hook,” he said. Povolny recommended checking authorised SSH keys on machines accessible to affected developers, rotating potentially exposed credentials, and reviewing logs for logins using unfamiliar keys. Developers often have access to source code, cloud accounts, and production systems, he said, making a compromised workstation a potential route to other enterprise resources. Phorion also advised checking the SSH key’s fingerprint rather than relying only on the comment svc-telemetry attached to it. Questions raised about extension security Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should treat extension marketplaces as part of the software supply chain. “An extension marketplace is effectively another software supply chain,” Kadakia said. “When malicious code can reach developers through what appears to be a legitimate, routine update, the traditional assumption that software from a trusted marketplace is safe starts to break down.” He recommended stronger publisher verification, checks on package integrity, and controls over which extensions and versions developers can install. Kadakia also called for extension allowlisting, controlled updates, endpoint monitoring, and restrictions on outbound connections. He said short-lived credentials, segregated development environments, and limited access to sensitive infrastructure could reduce the impact of a compromised developer machine. Cursor said it removed the malicious versions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, audited access, rotated keys, and rebuilt the marketplace before restoring the service.

Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29. The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server.

title: Why do we keep testing employees for yesterday’s phishing attacks
raw_text: “Yesterday’s price is not today’s price,” a phrase Fat Joe popularized in 2021 , reminds us that what worked yesterday may not deliver the same value today. In cybersecurity, this matters when we continue to assess employees against familiar phishing techniques while attackers use AI to craft more convincing, personalized messages. Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks? AI -enabled “phishing landscape” The traditional tell-tale signs of phishing which we used to train employees for are becoming less dependable. Generative AI can help attackers produce convincing messages, personalize lures and improve the quality of their communication. This does not mean every phishing campaign uses AI in reality, but it raises the bar for what employees may encounter . A 2025 report by SC Media covering Egress research found that 75% of the phishing kits examined on dark-web markets advertised AI capabilities, while 82% offered deepfake features. These figures relate to the kits analyzed, rather than all phishing activity, but they show that AI-enabled features are appearing in tools available to criminals. Add this to the spike in recent phishing attacks with AI prompt injections and you realize quickly the landscape has morphed. This matters for awareness programs. If employees are mainly taught to look for spelling mistakes, generic greetings or suspicious formatting, they may be less prepared for a message that uses familiar names, relevant business context and professional language when attackers use AI to craft them. Training needs to emphasize verification in addition to simply recognition and unexpected requests should be checked through a trusted channel, even when the message appears legitimate. Click rates are not everything Phishing simulations often produce a straightforward headline and statistics: the percentage of recipients who clicked a link, entered credentials and deleted or reported the message. They are easy metrics to communicate, compare and track over time and also to present to Senior Management in meetings but it provides only one part of the picture. Imagine two groups with the same click rate. In one, employees who suspect a message report it quickly, allowing the security team to investigate, detect other people who may have received it and warn other recipients. In the other, people delete the message or ignore it without reporting it. The click rates may look identical, but the organization’s ability to detect a real campaign is different. Reporting rates and time to report therefore deserve more attention. Security teams should understand whether employees use the approved reporting channel, how quickly suspicious messages reach analysts and whether those reports lead to effective action. The National Cyber Security Centre’s guidance on phishing provides practical advice on recognizing and reporting suspicious messages and organizations should have this on their website or HR portals. As I have seen in multiple simulations I have conducted, results also need careful interpretation. A test is a controlled exercise, not a guarantee of how someone will behave during a real attack, which could depend on the recipient’s state of mind. Employees may recognize familiar templates or learn the patterns used in repeated campaigns. Clicking a simulated link also does not automatically mean someone would compromise the organization in a real incident. The objective should be to identify weaknesses and improve security, not to rank employees by how often they pass or fail, and this should reflect in the way messages about failure are passed on. Test the response and the person Phishing simulations should evolve alongside the threats they are intended to represent. Scenarios should reflect realistic business situations, including unexpected document sharing, supplier requests and attempts to impersonate trusted colleagues instead of clicking links or supplying credentials only. Employees should learn how to verify unusual requests and report suspected attacks without fear of embarrassment or punishment. From experience, this may have many moving parts, like custom mailboxes, a departure from the simulation norm and multiple levels of approval before exercises like this can be done but it’s worth the effort. Security teams should also evaluate what happens after a suspicious message arrives. How quickly is it reported? Can analysts identify and contact other recipients who possibly responded to the message? Can the organization remove the message from inboxes, block malicious infrastructure and investigate potential account compromise? These questions connect awareness testing to operational readiness. The same principle applies to incident exercises. Security, IT, finance and relevant business teams should know what to do when a real phishing attack succeeds, which it inevitably will, someday. A program that improves reporting and response can deliver value even when it cannot prevent every employee from clicking. AI will continue to change how phishing messages are created and delivered and security awareness must change with it. The question is whether the organization can verify suspicious activity, detect an attack and limit its impact when the message looks entirely legitimate and is prone to being clicked as a result. Yesterday’s tests can still teach useful lessons but should not define tomorrow’s readiness.

Having conducted multiple phishing simulations and one in October, 2026, I believe we need to ask a harder question: are we preparing people for the phishing attacks they are likely to face today, or testing their ability to recognize or remember the warning signs we have taught them to expect? What happens when those warning signs don’t apply or they face novel attacks?

title: Who approves the files that control your AI coding assistant?
raw_text: A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions. Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine? The issue has moved beyond hypothetical repository poisoning. In an October 8 analysis of agent-skill distribution , StepSecurity revisited the June Miasma campaign, which planted AI-tool and editor configuration in a Microsoft repository without modifying application source. The configuration was intended to trigger credential harvesting through developer tooling. The October publication describes an inventory product, but the underlying campaign illustrates a wider operational problem: merging a configuration change can distribute execution instructions to the people working in that repository. StepSecurity also reports that the commit carried a skip-CI flag and a backdated timestamp, and that it moved code execution from package install to folder open. A control that runs only in the build pipeline never sees that path. The first reliable checkpoint is the pull request, and it needs a person who knows what the file can trigger. I recommend giving these changes a named owner and an enforceable review path. An organization should be able to identify who approved a hook, what the approval covered and where the approved version is allowed to run. Review the behavior behind the filename A repository file can serve several purposes. It may describe a coding convention, direct an agent toward a script, register a tool or arrange for a command to run at a lifecycle event. Those differences matter more than the extension. A Markdown instruction is not automatically executable code. It can nevertheless influence an agent that has permission to execute commands. A JSON setting may directly register a shell command. Review should establish the mechanism, the trigger and the authority available when it fires. Skills show why the filename is a poor guide. StepSecurity notes that a skill’s allowed-tools field can let the agent use listed tools without a permission prompt during the turn that invokes the skill, and that Claude Code’s documentation says workspace trust does not gate that field. A SKILL.md file is Markdown, so in a pull request it tends to be reviewed like a README. Anthropic’s current hooks reference states that command hooks run with the user’s permissions. It also distinguishes interactive workspace trust from noninteractive operation: settings-file hooks in a repository can run in a noninteractive session without the trust dialog shown to an interactive user. The exact behavior depends on the configuration surface and session type. A control tested at a developer’s terminal should therefore be retested in the automated workflow that uses the same repository. The same page names practical mitigations. Before scripting a noninteractive run over a repository nobody on the team wrote, review its .claude settings files, start the run in bare mode or turn hooks off for that run. Administrators can also use the managed-hooks-only setting so that user, project, local and plugin hooks are blocked. Which of these fits depends on the organization’s tooling, and each should be tested rather than assumed. For a proposed setup hook, the reviewer should be able to trace the command to its script and dependencies. If the script downloads another program, determine how that program is selected and verified. If it reads credentials or accesses the network, ask why the setup step needs those capabilities. These questions should accompany the change while its author can explain the intent. Discovering them after distribution leaves every affected developer to make an individual trust decision. Make ownership enforceable Engineering productivity teams are often best placed to maintain shared coding-assistant configuration. Security should define the conditions that require a second reviewer, such as adding executable hooks, broadening network access or invoking a new external tool. The application team remains responsible for whether the integration belongs in its workflow. This need not create an approval queue for every formatting preference. Define the behavioral changes that warrant scrutiny and route those changes to people who understand the tooling. GitHub’s code-owner documentation explains how ownership rules work with required reviews. A CODEOWNERS file alone does not make its approval mandatory; the corresponding branch protection must require it. GitHub also recommends protecting the ownership file itself. Apply the chosen mechanism to the agent configuration and the scripts it invokes. Protecting a settings file while leaving its referenced helper script outside the review rule creates an obvious gap. Check the effective rule with a sample pull request rather than relying on the presence of a policy file. Allow legitimate changes to move quickly through a known path. The reviewer should receive a concise explanation of the trigger, required access and expected side effects. A hook that formats changed files should not need the same justification as one that contacts an external service or modifies a user’s global configuration. Check what the developer environment actually loads Repository review covers only part of the environment. Developers can also install shared skills, plugins and user-level configuration outside a project. An approved repository may therefore run alongside additional instructions that its maintainers have never reviewed. Establish a baseline for the supported tools and launch methods. Record the origins and versions of approved additions, and provide a way to inspect the effective configuration. When local copies differ, compare the content before deciding that the difference is malicious or harmless. Microsoft’s Workspace Trust guidance for Visual Studio Code describes Restricted Mode, which limits features that can execute workspace content. It also warns that a malicious extension can ignore that boundary. Workspace trust is a useful control within its documented scope; it should be paired with a deliberate extension policy and an environment appropriate to the repository being inspected. Use unfamiliar repositories in an isolated environment without routinely mounted production credentials. Avoid treating a container as sufficient isolation if it inherits the developer’s secrets or access to the host. Review those connections explicitly. For approved daily work, make the safe setup practical. Publish maintained configurations, explain how to request an addition and provide a clean inspection workflow. If compliance requires developers to reconstruct their environment manually every morning, it will be difficult to sustain. Test the approval path before trusting it Run a benign exercise in a disposable repository and isolated environment. Add a hook that writes a harmless marker file. Check whether the pull request reaches the intended owner, whether an unapproved change can merge and whether the installed tool permits the marker action under the documented launch conditions. Repeat the exercise through the noninteractive route if the organization uses one. Then change only the referenced helper script. That second change tests whether the review boundary covers behavior as well as configuration. The result should identify which controls prevented execution and which merely recorded it. A scanner alert, required review and runtime restriction perform different jobs. Record the gaps without presenting one as a substitute for all the others. Three questions make a workable first review. Who can merge a change to the files that steer our coding assistants? Does that rule also cover every script those files call? Which of our automated jobs run the assistant over code we did not write, and do they apply the same trust checks as a developer’s terminal? For security leadership, the useful measure is whether changes capable of altering execution reach the right reviewer before distribution, and whether the working environment matches the approved scope. Start with one supported coding tool and one engineering team. Ask them to demonstrate who can change its behavior, how that change is approved and what happens when someone tries to bypass the process.
summary: A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions. Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine?

title: What a security strategy that survives 2027 looks like
raw_text: Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity. “AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.” In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment. “That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. Done well, security becomes one of the reasons a product can launch sooner.” As for the rising tide of AI agents entering enterprise workflows, Koppen says that “identity controls are central” to his 2027 security strategy. “Across the industry, more activity on enterprise networks now comes from AI agents, bots, and automated workflows, and most traditional security controls were designed with a human user in mind,” he explains. “That’s why we’re applying the same rigorous verification to these identities that we apply to people.” Of course, Koppen, like other seasoned security leaders, knows his IT security strategy must evolve to address more than just AI. Geopolitics, the anticipated arrival of quantum computing, and increasingly interconnected systems, are also changing the threat landscape and attack surface — sometimes in radical ways — and should prompt strategic changes, too. That in turn is putting pressure on CISOs to rethink their practices, policies, and approaches as we head toward a new year likely to be at least as wild of a ride as 2026 has been. “CISOs realize they need to transform, because their current state isn’t working. And it’s going to be a pretty significant transformation over the next few years for CISOs to be successful,” says Omar Khawaja, a CISO, a faculty member at Carnegie Mellon University’s CISO program, and a board member at HITRUST and FAIR Institute. Of course, transformation, as always, is a work in progress, Khawaja says; as a result many security execs are still working out what needs to change in 2027 and how to make those changes happen. Still, Khawaja, Koppen, and others stress that transformation is not an option; the safety of the organization depends on strategic evolution from its cybersecurity teams. So what exactly needs to change? Security leaders point to specific elements that won’t work as well in the year ahead and what needs to be in place instead to more adequately secure the organization in 2027 and beyond. Static credentials need to go Koppen believes static credentials are on their way out. “No matter how strict the policy, passwords still end up looking like a favorite sports team or the current season with an exclamation point at the end. That makes them trivial targets for brute-force attacks,” he says, noting that his company eliminated passwords across its 22,000 employees and contractors and is now extending its passwordless standard to its B2B customers. More manual SOC work must be automated The new command for security teams is to move at machine speed. “We’re not able to deal with attacks and vulnerabilities manually anymore. AI is making that impossible,” says Florida State University CISO Bill Hunkapiller. His security strategy reflects this new reality. He has been implementing autonomous agents to replace routine security operations tasks, and his 2027 plans call for expanding the number of tasks handled by machines. Most CISOs are on this path. The State of Incident Response Readiness from Sygnia found that 32% of organizations have extensive AI use across most or all threat detection and incident response (IR) activities, up from 25% in 2025. And 63% expect to have extensive AI use in place for threat detection and IR activities in 2027. Generic severity scores are out, risk ratings tailored to the organization are in Equifax’s Koppen declares that generic severity scores are no longer effective. “A vendor’s ‘critical’ rating doesn’t know if a system holds sensitive data, is externally facing, or sits behind other controls,” he says, noting that Equifax has its own quantitative risk engine that factors in that context so its teams “can focus on issues that pose real risk to the business.” Hunkapiller, who is also chief privacy officer and an adjunct professor at FSU, also sees a need to understand how common vulnerabilities and exposures pose a risk to his organization in particular, rather than relying on ratings. To that end, he’s exploring services that could create a digital twin of his environment to simulate how hackers could exploit vulnerabilities in his organization. This service would give Hunkapiller near-real-time information on which vulnerabilities pose the most significant risks to FSU, allowing him to accurately prioritize fixing those quickly, he says. Thus far, he’s impressed with the capability, saying it’s like “attack surface management on steroids.” Continuous patching is now the goal Security used to have Patch Tuesday, a moniker that reflected the regularly scheduled work of applying newly released fixes to software flaws. Although security teams today may not adhere to Tuesday specifically for the work, many still patch on a set schedule — and many still take weeks to patch. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report puts the median time to remediate known exploited vulnerabilities at 43 days, up from 32 days in 2025. That won’t fly in 2027 , says Hugh Thompson, program chair for the RSA Conference. “We used to do patching very methodically. If a patch came out for a system, we didn’t want to roll it out right away [for fear] it could break something. So we took time and tested it out and scheduled the work. That’s not going to work now, because the speed at which these AI attackers can take advantage of vulnerabilities or discover new ones is greater than ever,” he says. “We need automation in patching.” Jason Rader, CISO for technology solutions and systems integrator Insight, has been accelerating his company’s patching program, bringing patch windows down to seven days for its most critical components — a significant accomplishment given the size of the IT environment and the number of patches being released. Still, he wants to do better, saying he’s aiming to increase speed for patching in all areas of the IT environment in 2027 and noting that he’d like to eventually get to continuous patching. Different treatment for agent and NHIs needs to end With AI agents doing more work that was, until recently, performed by humans, it’s becoming increasingly clear that security can’t treat machine identities — whether agents or systems or APIs — differently than humans, Rader says. To that end, he’s already “managing agents like people,” applying equally diligent attention to managing identity and associated permissions — and, thus, access to data and systems — to ensure that each entity can access only what is appropriate for its role. This includes managing machine identities throughout the lifecycle of those machines, just as security should for human workers, and applying proper governance, Rader adds. Agility and adaptability must be part of the 2027 strategy Some CISOs still take a set-and-forget approach to policies, procedures, and standards, says Prakash Venkata, a cyber, data, and tech risk partner at PWC and the firm’s security, risk, and engineering practice leader. That approach never worked well, as there has always been a need to improve and evolve policies, procedures, and standards as the threat landscape and the attack surface changed, Venkata explains. But the pace of change now is so fast that CISOs need to build agility and adaptability into their strategies simply to keep up and meet industry standards. Thompson likewise preaches the need for more agility in security strategies and advises security leaders to “be prepared for agility more than we had to or could stomach in the past because problems will emerge that you can’t anticipate.” He notes, too, that CISOs need to work with other departments, such as procurement, to bring that needed agility to security. For example, if the CISO needs to quickly buy and implement new technology to reduce a recently identified risk or defend against an emerging threat, CISOs will need procurement procedures to move as fast as security must move. Detached AI security and governance strategies become obsolete There has been a rise of AI governance and security strategies that are detached from the organization’s overall governance and security strategy, says James Lyne, CEO of SANS, a security training and certification organization. Lyne believes that the attention on AI governance and security is critical. However, he thinks having fully segregated AI governance and security strategies will be increasingly detrimental in 2027 and beyond. That’s because they’re not different and separate from enterprise governance and security. “An AI app exposed to malicious inputs is an app security problem,” he says. “AI agents accessing unauthorized things is a privilege management and operation security issue [no less than] if people had unauthorized access.” To ensure organizations have an effective, coordinated approach to governance and security capable of protecting the entire organization, where elements work together with no siloes or redundancies, CISOs and their organizations need a unified security strategy that addresses all actors — “whether they’re human, software services, or AI agents, or automated workflows,” he says.
summary: Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity. “AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.” In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment. “That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says.

title: Government-backed open property initiative enters new phase
raw_text:
The Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology (CFIT) has moved its open property project to the next phase, with real-world cases to be tested.

After completing roadmaps on developing open finance, digital ID, and small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) access to finance, the government-backed CFIT moved its focus on open property a year ago.

Through a roadmap, CFIT and the open property coalition are attempting to transform the home buying and selling sector. The government wants to transform the archaic home buying and selling process, which costs the economy nearly £1bn a year. CFIT is tasked with bringing together the public and private sector organisations required to make this happen successfully.

The open property coalition brings together expertise from across the entire homebuying chain, including mortgage lenders, property technology providers, conveyancers, estate agents, government departments and regulators.

Earlier this year, the coalition began identifying a consensus on what it can do and map it. Part of this involved identifying the data sets that were being used by the market and data clusters, which are reusable collections of data which could be used for various purposes.

Now it will move to testing out approaches that could be adopted by the sector. Coalition participants include the Conveyancing Information Executive, Connells Group, Council of Property Search Organisations, HSBC, Lloyds Banking Group, and NatWest.

The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Technology; the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; HM Land Registry; and the Digital Property Market Steering group are closely watching developments,

“Over the coming months, coalition members will work together to develop and test real-world use cases, explore how existing standards and systems can work together, and identify the practical requirements for wider adoption across a more trusted and interoperable property ecosystem,” said CFIT. “The evidence generated will help to inform the wider work of government, the Digital Property Market Steering Group and industry.”

Read more: CFIT is ‘shaking up business models’ with UK government backing.

Anna Wallace, CEO of CFIT, said the latest phase is a sign that stakeholders are uniting: “The breadth of industry support for the next phase of CFIT’s Open Property Coalition is a significant step forward. This announcement reflects growing alignment between industry, government and the Digital Property Market Steering Group on what needs to change, and we now have a real opportunity to turn our ambition to create a digital and more efficient homebuying process into reality.”

Brad Fordham, head of mortgage distribution and underwriting at NatWest bank, said: “Buying a home is one of the biggest financial decisions our customers make, but securing a mortgage is only one part of a much wider and often complex journey.”

He highlighted that tech plays a key role in reducing the complexity: “Lenders rely on trusted information from across the property ecosystem, so there is a significant opportunity to use smart data and digital technology to make that information easier to verify and share securely.”

The coalition approach ensures that ideas can be tested across the entire homebuying sector, added Fordham: “Open property brings together the organisations needed to explore how that can work across the whole transaction, rather than improving individual stages in isolation. By testing these approaches in practice, we can help build the evidence and confidence needed to create a simpler, more transparent homebuying experience for customers.”

Travis Scholes, commercial director at conveyancing services firm LMS, said: “The foundations for a more connected homebuying process are already being established across the market. The opportunity now is to connect the organisations, expertise and infrastructure needed to drive adoption at scale.”

title: UK to face AI-powered cyber attacks within two years, warns NCSC
raw_text:
The UK will face AI-powered attacks from nation-states and criminal groups targeting critical national infrastructure within two years, according to an assessment published today by the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of GCHQ.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) by hostile states and crime groups is expected to increase the scale and speed of ransomware attacks, social engineering and the exploitation of vulnerabilities.

The NCSC said Russia and China will routinely use AI-powered cyber tools to achieve their geopolitical goals.

It also predicts that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on critical national infrastructure in the UK.

In a worst-case scenario, the UK could face automated attacks from frontier AI capable of self-replicating and conducting cyber attacks at will.

The UK is at a point of “enormous consequence” and faces “a moment of choice” over how to respond to AI-powered threats, the NCSC’s CEO, Richard Horne, is expected to say in a speech today.

“When food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under … we may have to explain that we saw the warning signs, understood the risks, and still didn’t make the right choices,” he will warn.

Organisations will need to make “significant” changes to protect critical systems and will no longer be able to rely on “technology on the cheap”.

That includes securing the technology that controls physical infrastructure, including electricity switches, dams, manufacturing lines, and heating and refrigeration controls, where investment in security and resilience has been less of a priority.

Cyber attacks on hundreds of refrigerators in French supermarkets, which destroyed millions of euros of food last month, show the exposure of countries to cyber risks is “huge”.

Military networks targeted

Military networks are subject to sustained, persistent attempts to penetrate communications by countries such as Russia, which is exploiting tactics developed in Ukraine against states and institutions.

Hybrid warfare campaigns are “escalating”, while intentionally falling below the threshold of armed conflict, according to the NCSC.

Despite the pressures of the Middle East conflict, Iran is still carrying out malicious cyber operations targeting the UK and individuals seen as a threat to the regime.

China is said to be best positioned to use AI for operations against UK critical national infrastructure and other strategic targets.

It represents the most “sophisticated and sustained” cyber challenge faced by the UK, according to the NCSC.

Unprecedented rise in cyber attacks

“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” Horne is expected to say.  

Organisations will need to make “different choices” with their technology. That means addressing past failures to adequately invest in security, not having technology unnecessarily connected to the internet and building greater resilience.

“We can be a nation where leaders of all organisations actively choose to invest with urgency … and where all organisations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought,” he will say.

Failing to make these choices will mean business leaders having to “look their investors, shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers in the eye and explain … when food isn’t on shelves, lights aren’t on, businesses have gone under”.

The AI security divide

AI has the potential to be one of the greatest opportunities in cyber defence, allowing technology companies to fix hundreds of vulnerabilities in a single update, the NCSC claims.

Organisations with mature cyber security programmes, robust governance and sufficient resources will be able to detect threats, prioritise vulnerabilities and automate their defences, according to the NCSC’s State of the cyber nation report.

Weaker organisations are likely to struggle to keep pace with AI-assisted attacks, creating a widening gap between resilient and vulnerable organisations.

Cost of cyber attacks to UK

The NCSC estimates that malicious cyber activity costs UK organisations an estimated £14.7bn every year.

The attack on Jaguar Land Rover had a direct impact on GDP, contributing to lower growth in the UK economy than expected.

The centre received 1,830 reports of cyber attacks during the past year, of which 80 were classed as nationally significant.

The bulk of state-backed attacks seen by the NCSC to date do not use advanced, autonomous AI, but exploit common vulnerabilities and exposures that are known to work, but that could change rapidly.

Cyber Shield

The NCSC’s warning comes as the government is investing in the UK’s defence and resilience capabilities, including the development of a national Cyber Shield that will use agentic AI to build a national-scale cyber defence capability.

A National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre will use AI to identify security vulnerabilities across critical national infrastructure and the economy.

title: Cold chain cyber attacks highlight lack of OT security in retail
raw_text:
A series of renewed cyber attacks on retail refrigeration systems has set alarm bells ringing across Europe, with reports of temperatures in some freezer units rising as high as 50C, causing ruined food to have to be dumped.

Although on a smaller scale, the latest incidents that took place across multiple countries are all strongly reminiscent of a serious incident that took place in France in October, which affected hundreds of branches of multiple supermarket chains, and come days after it emerged US authorities are investigating a series of similar attacks that targeted freezers at US military bases.

In Ireland, Musgrave, which backs the nationwide SuperValu chain, confirmed a small number of stores had been impacted by an incident targeting certain refrigeration equipment models.

A spokesperson said the situation was now returning to normal and that it was working with suppliers and cyber specialists on its investigation.

James Neilson, global senior vice-president at Opswat, said: “This is the second time in three weeks, and it won’t be the last. When a remote management layer controls a physical process, it becomes a single point of failure for an entire retail estate, and one compromise can hit many stores at once.

“The scale is smaller than in France, but for each affected store the damage is just as real. Stock has to be destroyed and replaced, suppliers and distribution centres must absorb a surge in demand, refrigeration technicians have to inspect and restore systems site by site, and retailers must reassure customers that what’s back on the shelves is safe.”

OT blind spot

In this instance, and as is often the case in cyber attacks involving critical sectors like energy and food distribution, connected operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) offer threat actors an easy means to cause maximum disruption.

Sweden’s Nationellt Cybersäkerhetscenter (NCSC) – which has been closely monitoring the incidents and working with victims – said the event showed how important it is to protect systems that control and monitor physical processes. Unlike more regularly updated IT environments, OT environments often include huge amounts of legacy technology that can be much harder, or even impossible, to patch when flaws emerge, leaving them highly vulnerable.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear, much of it installed by facilities contractors who rarely loop in the security team,” said Tom Hegel, distinguished threat researcher and research lead at SentinelOne.

“Grocery margins are thin and stock perishes within hours, so any disruption hurts quickly and in public. The gap between a nuisance and a serious incident often comes down to how much control a victim has exposed to the internet. With thousands of these interfaces still online, I expect more incidents like this.”

Indeed, scans of publicly visible refrigeration units conducted by Forescout in the wake of the October attacks in France found almost 13,000 vulnerable services across over 6,000 public IP addresses in 99 countries all over the world, with France, Greece and Italy particularly badly exposed.

Among some of the bigger names in the field, it found over 7,000 at-risk Copeland/DIxell XWEB services, 4,500 Danfoss StoreView services, 550 Copeland Site Supervisor services, and 500 Carel pCOWeb services.

Concerningly, said Forescout, 80% of scanned Danfoss AK-SM 800A StoreView services – a software platform that provides a user interface (UI) for web access to AK-SM800A refrigeration monitors – were affected by known vulnerabilities. Danfoss equipment was heavily targeted during the October attacks in France.

Russia link?

Although Moscow has consistently denied any official involvement, hacktivist groups based in Russia and operating in its geopolitical interests have claimed at least 20 attacks against refrigeration systems so far this year, according to Forescout.

Forescout’s researchers said the most active groups behind these attacks were NoName057(16) and the associated Z-Pentest Alliance group.

NoName057(16) has previously been linked to a Kremlin-funded non-governmental organisation (NGO) called the Center for the Study and Network Monitoring of the Youth Environment, and allegedly operates the Z-Pentest Alliance in collaboration with a group known as the Cyber Army of Russia Reborn.

Although NoName057(16) has tended to specialise in distributed denial of service attacks, Z-Pentest Alliance has been seen focusing on OT environments at critical organisations.

However, SentinelOne’s Hegel said that in this scenario, attribution was harder than it seemed.

“An attacker who logs in to an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind, with no malware to analyse and few clues beyond an IP address that probably leads to a rented server,” he said. “A teenager and an intelligence service would look much the same from the defender’s side.”

“These types of attacks typically fall into three main categories: ransomware extortion, political/ideological hacktivism, or nation-state level cyber operations,” said Hegel. “Ransomware groups usually try to get paid, and hacktivists usually want the public credit.

“In this case, neither has happened, which makes it start to look like the low-cost, deniable sabotage Europe has been dealing with for several years, from damaged undersea cables to warehouse arson and GPS jamming.”

Regardless, he added, the advice to retailers in the UK – which does not yet seem to have been targeted – and across Europe, is to take refrigeration system controllers off the internet, put vendor access behind strong authentication, and audit and replace any end-of-life units that no longer get updates.

“Retailers don’t need to know who did it before they act,” he said.

title: Who controls the technology we depend on?
raw_text:
Being dependent on another country’s technology and support carries risk, however close the relationship appears. Yet when we discuss nation state cyber threats, we tend to focus on hostile actors breaking into our systems. We should also examine who controls the systems we already depend on.

For the UK, that means facing our reliance on US technology. Cloud infrastructure, business software and security services are deeply embedded in government and commerce. The CMA has identified significant market power held by Microsoft and Amazon in cloud services, alongside barriers that make switching difficult. This is a resilience issue as well as a competition issue.

An alliance is a political relationship, and political relationships change. Continued US support and alignment with UK interests should no longer be treated as an unquestioned planning assumption. We need to assess what happens when commercial decisions, government policy or geopolitical pressure affect access to essential technology.

Starlink in Ukraine makes that question painfully practical. In February, Ukraine introduced terminal authorisation to counter Russian use of the service. On 14 October, Ukrainian officials reported that restrictions affecting services used by military drones had disrupted missions without warning. Reuters reported that SpaceX had not immediately commented and the reason for the restrictions was unclear.

We should be careful about attributing motives. Nevertheless, the lesson we draw is that effective technology can become a critical dependency whose operating conditions are controlled elsewhere. For government, defence and critical national infrastructure, that should prompt some uncomfortable questions about sovereignty and continuity.

Where is our data? Who administers the service? Which jurisdictions govern the provider? Who can alter access, support or functionality? Crucially, could we continue operating if that service became unavailable? A second supplier offers limited protection if it depends on the same underlying infrastructure or jurisdiction.

Meanwhile, espionage remains a persistent threat. The NCSC’s warning about Integrity Technology Group describes activity combining AI tools, compromised devices and manual exploitation. Organisations need to understand why their information, research or supply chain position might interest a state actor, including the access they provide to others.

Boards should bring these risks together. Technical protection, supplier assurance and geopolitical exposure need shared ownership across security, procurement, legal and operations. Strong authentication, controlled access, protected logging and network separation remain essential. So do realistic exercises that test loss of a major provider and the ability to detect an intruder using legitimate tools.

AI adoption adds further dependencies. Organisations should know which providers process sensitive information, what access their systems receive and whether an alternative could actually be deployed. An exit plan that has never been tested offers little assurance.

Public-private cooperation matters: act on NCSC guidance, report incidents and exchange intelligence through trusted channels. Government also has a role in supporting domestic capability and reducing barriers to switching.

Businesses cannot remove every international dependency. They can identify concentrations of risk, challenge assumptions about continued support and invest in workable alternatives. Resilience requires understanding what we control, what we depend on, and what happens when circumstances change.
