title: Gartner on AI ROI: A Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
There are plenty of horror stories of artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives not only failing to deliver a measurable return on investment (ROI), but also experiencing out-of-control costs.

When asked whether Gartner was seeing any indication that its CIO and IT leadership clients were getting a measurable ROI on AI, Yogesh Bhatt, said: “The straight answer to that is no. Most enterprises are actually trapped in a severe profit and loss (P&L) gap.”

As enterprises start deploying more and more autonomous agentic AI, Bhatt says compliance-based governance is no longer enough to ensure IT costs are kept under control. “What is required is linking of AI FinOps directly to technical run-time controls. That's an urgent board priority.” He says some organisations are unaware of their AI costs until they see the invoice.

While organisations are still trying to experiment with AI and AI agents, in Bhatt’s experience, they are not realising the value perspective of those agents. “There is cost attribution  and most IT leaders and enterprises are hiding behind colourful dashboards which show projected hours saved as productivity gains. But the challenge is that these gains are failing to show up in the financial statements.”

Unmonitored token spend is primarily attributed to AI agents continually retrying a task and shadow AI. Bhatt said these quietly destroy the expected margins. Gartner predicts that by 2030, failing to adopt adaptive run-time controls will triple AI deployment cost”

As organisations build more complex systems using multiple AI agents, Bhatt warns that costs still increase, even when token costs are reduced.

In the past IT leaders were presented with the idea of data democratisation where business intelligence tools are deployed widely to enable workers to make more informed, data-driven decisions. Bhatt says AI presents what he calls a more “non-deterministic world”. He says organisations tend to overestimate how easily the soft productivity gained from AI can be turned  into hard profits. At the same tim he says they tend to underestimate how quickly unmonitored agentic workflows burn through the corporate budget. “Soft productivity metrics don't pay your bills,” he says.

Bhatt says CIOs should manage the ROI across all AI and agentic AI initiatives in their organisation. “They have to evolve their AI governance from passive administrative compliance into a more active runtime financial execution, which is embedded directly at the AI gateway layer itself.”

He urges CIOs to tie the ROI directly to profit and loss metrics. An example could be measuring sales bids to profit conversion or the volume of automated contract renewals.

Looking at run-time controls, he says: “ “You need to look at enforcing instance tagging, tracking who is using the token, for what purpose, and where they are actually using it. Then there is the invocation path of the AI agent, to trace where all the cost is being proliferated.”

“Currently, we are all looking at raw model cost only,” he adds. The AI gateway needs instrumentation and the ability to separate the raw model cost from demonstrated value. 

He says AI is not hitting a financial wall because the technology lacks power. Instead, it's failing because enterprises are managing autonomous AI with outdated passive compliance frameworks. “To capture real value, IT leaders have to bridge the profit and loss gap. The ROI has to be tied to P&L, because that's when you start seeing value.” The bottom line, is to move from from lagging indicators and alerts to active policy run-time control which directly talks to an AI gateway layer and provides what Bhatt sees as “hard budget blocks”, with the ability to downshift dynamically to lower cost models when needed.

title: Wiltshire Ark datacentre project faces potential judicial review
raw_text:
A Wiltshire-based campaign group is mulling a judicial review to reverse plans for a seventh datacentre at Ark Data Centres’ Spring Park campus near Corsham. The group – Neston and Westwells Action Group (NWAG) – said flood risk evidence was not supplied.

Wiltshire Council granted full planning permission in October and cites more than 1,000 objections to the scheme on the council’s planning portal.

The consent allows a freestanding datacentre building plus energy, power and water infrastructure on the 18-acre Donkey Field site, which sits in view of a nearby retirement village. Objections include potential for noise, traffic and reduced air quality as well as broader quality of life concerns (see below).

Ark already runs five datacentres on the site and is building a sixth. The seventh would be the first outside the wire of former Ministry of Defence (MoD) land at Corsham, which hosts Crown Hosting Data Centres, a Cabinet Office-Ark joint venture that stores government data to top secret classification. The 18.7m-tall building would sit within 50 metres of local homes, on a field above a disused mine linked to an MoD Cold War bunker. The village suffered a once-in-a-generation flood in 2014.

NWAG said it was not opposed to datacentres or economic growth. Its argument turns on whether evidence showing the site could be drained safely was in place before consent was given.

Flood risk in dispute

NWAG said infiltration testing, groundwater monitoring, hydraulic modelling and the behaviour of runoff during severe rainfall remained unresolved, despite the council concluding the development would not increase flood risk. It also questioned advice given to councillors, which said testing that steers development away from areas at higher flood risk no longer applied to surface water flooding.

“The fundamental question is what evidence existed at the point of decision to demonstrate that the site could be safely drained without increasing flood risk elsewhere,” said an NWAG spokesperson. “Further conditioned investigations should verify an established solution. They should not be the means by which we discover afterwards whether a solution existed in the first place.”

The group must lodge any challenge by 14 November 2026 and said it is still gauging public support and funding pledges before deciding whether to proceed. Its position, it said, is “prove it before you approve it”. NWAG has separately asked the council to clarify how a proposed construction logistics use on adjacent land known as Donkey Fields was authorised, saying it could not find it in the application description.

The dispute comes as the Burnham government puts its mark on the datacentre debate, with its recent launch of a datacentre covenant that makes priority grid connections for datacentres conditional on strict tests around community investment, local jobs and water supplies.

The covenant calls on developers to co-design local benefit plans with residents and to protect local water and environmental resources. For the datacentre industry, the case is a live test of the evidential bar councils will demand before consenting schemes, as ministers push to accelerate construction of critical national infrastructure.

Anatomy of the objections

Wiltshire Council said objections were carefully considered alongside technical assessments and planning policy, and that conditions would address drainage, environmental protection, transport and other impacts.

We analysed the 1,141 comments on the council’s planning portal and found opinion runs heavily against the scheme:

  • Against: 1,050 (1,042 objections and eight petition objections)
  • In support: 15 (14 statements of support and one petition in support)
  • Other: 76 (comments, conditional no-objections and mixed positions)

The objections split between technical critiques and complaints about quality of life. The flood risk concerns underpinning the possible legal challenge appeared in fewer comments than noise or amenity complaints. Many raised several issues, so the figures overlap:

  • Flooding and drainage – 354 comments
  • Ecology and wildlife – 517
  • Air quality – 493
  • Power and energy – 111
  • Noise – 630
  • Traffic – 455
  • Broader quality-of-life – 782

The shortest submissions were blunt – “No”, “Outrageous”, “Not needed”. Others carried professional weight and were lengthy. David Palmer, a chartered civil engineer and fellow of the Institution of Civil Engineers with 37 years in flood risk management, wrote about shortcomings in flood risk assessment.

Morgyn Davies of NWAG wrote that the application contained “extraordinarily little new information … [and was] primarily a rehash of all previous documentation”, with flood risk questions “not addressed”.

Support was thin but present. One village resident wrote: “The need for this infrastructure is key to the nation.” Commercial property consultancy CBRE backed the scheme in a letter of support, as did a handful of other residents.

title: Workday Rising: Humans and AI must labour cheek by jowl
raw_text:
There was a whole lot of hugging on stage at the recent Workday Rising event in Las Vegas. During the keynote presentation, executives often greeted each other with an embrace, and they even stressed their predilection for hugging. Whether intentional or not, this human connection matched Workday’s key message of the event: the modern world of work is fast becoming agent-enabled, but humans remain crucial to success.

“We envision a situation where humans and agents work side by side,” said Workday CEO Aneel Bhusri during his firm’s keynote presentation. “That is the role we’re orienting in now. That’s the role of the future. The goal: how do we offload repetitive tasks from teams to focus on what only humans can do – that judgement, that creativity, that leadership?”

Workday’s vision is a harmonious blend of humans and artificial intelligence (AI) agents – lots of them. During the keynote, Bhusri outlined how his company has pushed 17 agents to production. These agents cover a range of areas, including a “talent acquisition agent” that searches for qualified candidates and coordinates interview scheduling, and a “developer agent” that allows IT professionals to generate applications and workflows using natural language prompts.

Of course, convincing employees that this new catalogue of agentic colleagues isn’t coming to steal their jobs is another issue altogether. Gerrit Kazmaier, president of product and technology at Workday, recognised during the keynote that most headlines today paint a far less harmonious picture of the rise of agentic AI.

“It’s one where the AI doesn’t amplify people; it replaces them,” he said. “It’s a situation where increasingly powerful AI behaves totally unpredictably. Where even the leaders building the most advanced frontier models are warning us about the risks of their very own creations. More than a quarter of American workers worry that technology will make their jobs obsolete. That is a new record, and I say that’s a sad record.”

Kazmaier and his senior colleagues hope Workday can change that record. Yes, the world of work is transforming, but that doesn’t have to be a bad thing. Rather than jobs with strict roles and responsibilities, the workplace of the future will be fluid and agile, where professionals fulfil tasks according to their skills, not their job titles. In this workplace transformation, Workday wants HR, finance and other line-of-business professionals to embrace agents.

“Jobs are going to change; there’s no question about it,” said Bhusri, recognising that professionals understandably fear the rate of change. “Jobs are being redefined into skills and roles that are very different than what they were pre-AI. But let’s embrace that. Let’s all of us within the audience learn AI, use the tools, embrace the opportunity.”

Refounding the company

During the event, Workday executives were eager to stress that the company is building agentic capabilities into its platform, rather than bolting them on. Like other tech firms responding to the rise of agents and application programming interfaces (APIs), the company is building an increasingly open platform with strong links to pioneer models, like Anthropic Claude.

A core component of this agentic strategy is Sana. It’s been a big 12 months for the AI platform, which Workday acquired in November 2025 and has spent the past year tweaking and integrating. In Las Vegas, it announced that Sana will sit at the core of the user experience for HR, finance and line-of-business professionals who interact with Workday.

Known as Workday Home, the Sana user interface lets professionals use natural language for help with key operational activities, such as completing tasks and making decisions. Sana orchestrates Workday agents to complete these activities. Bhusri said in his keynote that this interactive approach lets users take control.

“For too long, enterprise software forced you to do the work, searching for apps, data and processes,” he said. “We’re flipping that script with Sana, the new front door to Workday. Instead of hunting through menus, instead of looking for the work you need to get done, you simply ask, like it’s a simple AI prompt.”

Workday also introduced Sana Concierge, a new HR and IT service agent that resolves employee requests, from onboarding and leave to password resets, before they become tickets. The new Sana Workday Home experience is available now. Sana Concierge is available to early adopter customers, with general availability expected in the first quarter of 2027.

For customers aiming to get a handle on Workday’s long-term roadmap, there was a lot to take in. A new Sana homepage, 17 agents, and a series of other releases and updates related to data platforms, security features and business intelligence. As Bhusri suggested in the keynote, Workday is eager to demonstrate its innovations.

“The theme of this conference is ‘Show, not tell’,” he said. “I’ve watched a lot of AI conferences recently; just a lot of slideware. The most slides you’re going to see are the ones from me, and I don’t have that many slides. You’re going to see a lot of products, and these aren’t products that are in the labs. These are mostly products that are already in production.”

As the world of work changes, Workday is transforming to develop the agentic innovations it believes its customers need. Bhusri, who co-founded the company in 2005 and stepped down as chief executive in 2024, returned as CEO in February 2026. He acknowledged that he’s overseen a hectic period of change since returning.

AI sits at the heart of this transformation. Bhusri sees the rise of emerging technology as an opportunity for Workday to shine in what he called the next chapter of the technology industry. To ensure his company is ready for this narrative shift, he’s spent the past nine months building an internal startup-like culture.

“We want to transform the enterprise,” he said during his keynote. “I don’t worry about the big companies like SAP and Oracle. Maybe I should, but I don’t. I still think they’re dinosaurs. I’ll always think that. They’re not bad people, but they’re out of date. Startups – that’s where it’s at, and that’s what we’re paying attention to.”

Bhusri said it’s best to portray this transformation as a “refounding” of Workday focused on AI, with a startup-like culture that’s set up for success. When asked by Computer Weekly during a media panel session to define what this organisation might look like 12 months from now, he said, “Leaner, faster.”

This journey has already begun. As part of its reorganisation, Workday announced a global workforce reduction of approximately 2.5% in September 2026, affecting about 500 employees. Bhusri addressed the cuts in the media session.

“There were, in some parts of the development organisation, 10 layers between me and the developer getting work done, and it was the individual contributors and developers themselves who said, ‘I can’t get anything done. There are too many layers of approval’.”

Delivering for customers

The priority for Workday now is to ensure its customers understand the firm’s fresh agentic direction. In a one-to-one interview with Computer Weekly at the event, Dean Arnold, Workday’s vice-president of AI platform, said he hoped customers would recognise the firm is meeting them with agentic solutions to help them solve their key business challenges.

“Even last year, we saw the proliferation of customers building agents,” he said. “People were saying, ‘I want more agents and AI, and I want it now.’ We’re still seeing that trend going on, but tokenomics and everything else is bringing it down to a rationalised field of, ‘Okay, what’s the outcome we’re after?’”

CIOs have spent the past 12 months reflecting on agentic hyperbole. Now, with the board eager to see the benefits of agentic explorations, digital leaders are focused on tokenomics and the discipline of measuring, pricing and optimising how AI models consume tokens to create business value.

Arnold believes the hard work that he and his colleagues have put into the Workday platform in the past 12 months will pay dividends for the business and its customers. “The way we’re delivering agents is an evolution from the way we spoke about them last year,” he said. “We’re moving from a chat-style interface agent to something that’s more interwoven into a natural part of how your business operates.”

The priority is to ensure Workday clients see the benefits. “We have to help our customers be enabled on the agents that we’re producing,” said Arnold. “Our agents are focused on their business problems. They should be aware that we’re ready to help them.”

One customer already taking steps in this direction is Hezha Guimond, vice-president for HR technology and integration at Anew Health. Her organisation is using Workday’s AI Talent Suite, particularly the “recruiting agent” and “candidate experience agent”, to identify and hire staff faster. Guimond told Computer Weekly at the event that she was impressed by the firm’s announcements, particularly regarding Sana.

“I love coming to Rising because I get an opportunity to connect with like-minded people and see what Workday’s roadmap looks like, which is exciting. You speak with other customers and realise you’re doing well. It’s such a great feeling because you come here, and you’re like, ‘Oh, we’re a lot further ahead than we thought’,” she said.

“Even before coming here, I’d already contacted our Workday account manager, who’s done some work for me on the investment, and I’ve already made it very clear that I want Sana. So, Sana for sure is something we’re getting in 2027, as well as Workday Extend,” which is the IT company’s development platform that lets customers build applications inside its ecosystem.

Adam Zaller, vice-president of global HR services at Cardinal Health, is another business leader impressed with Workday’s strategic direction. His company went live with the platform in 2010 and has continued to evolve its implementation, including through agentic services. Like Guimond, he was impressed by Sana and believes the company’s AI-enabled developments complement his organisation’s ongoing digital transformation.

“It’s more affirmation that they’re on the path that I want them to be on. I’m pleased with how they’re progressing. I like the approach they’re taking. It’s not everything all at once. I wouldn’t call it a slow pace. It’s a nice, reasonable pace,” he said.

“Everything else is moving at light speed. I like the company that’s running my people data to make well-thought-out moves. And I think they’re doing that. I really like how they’re operating. Also, I’ve been pretty pleased to see the progress with Sana. I think Sana is something that’s really going to be a game-changer.”

title: Belfast journalists subjected to unlawful spying cannot claim costs over PSNI failures
raw_text:
Two Belfast journalists placed under unlawful police surveillance expressed “deep disappointment” after the Court of Appeal found that police cannot be sanctioned for “late and inadequate disclosures” of evidence that led to two court hearings having to be abandoned.

Investigative journalists Barry McCaffrey and Trevor Birney brought a case to the Court of Appeal in October, seeking to recover wasted costs after the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) repeatedly withheld and delayed the disclosure of important evidence, in some cases until the night before a court hearing.

A panel of five judges at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) previously found it had no statutory powers to impose sanctions against police forces or intelligence agencies if they delay or fail to follow orders from the tribunal to disclose relevant evidence.

The judge acknowledged that the five IPT judges had previously found there was a strong case for the tribunal to have powers to award costs “against respondents, where there has been expenditure wasted as a result of their conduct and where, in particular, orders of the tribunal are persistently breached”.

The Court of Appeal found that the tribunal had no power to award costs under the existing statutory framework. The Investigatory Powers Act did not create a costs jurisdiction and there was no provision to award costs in the tribunal rules, it said.

The court also rejected an alternative argument from the journalists that compensation awards could be increased to reflect their legal costs and found no error in law by the IPT for its decision not to increase the compensation already awarded.

The tribunal heard in March 2024 that the PSNI had failed to disclose surveillance operations against the two journalists until the night before scheduled court hearings, in breach of the tribunal’s orders. 

In one case, the PSNI served key evidence at 11:19pm the night before a court hearing, forcing the journalists’ lawyers to work through the night, and leaving no time to properly consider the evidence the next day.

On another occasion, the PSNI failed to disclose a Directed Surveillance Order against the two journalists until the morning of a court hearing, when the journalists’ legal representative was allowed to take notes from it but not allowed a copy.

Commenting on the Court of Appeal decision, Birney said the court’s interpretation meant that public authorities “can obstruct, delay and breach tribunal orders with financial impunity”.

“The IPT itself described this lack of power as an unsatisfactory outcome,” he said. “It cannot be right that state agencies can waste public funds and frustrate the course of justice without facing consequences.”

“This case began because our homes were unlawfully searched to protect state secrets and expose our confidential sources,” he said. “We proved the PSNI acted unlawfully. The IPT ruled in December 2024 that the PSNI unlawfully ordered an undercover surveillance operation that attempted to identify a confidential source who had supplied information to the journalists. 

The tribunal judgment ordered the PSNI to pay £4,000 each in damages to Birney and McCaffrey, matching damages previously awarded by the European Court of Human Rights to journalists who were subject to state surveillance to identify their sources.
